content: Anaphylaxis is a severe hypersensitivity reaction that occurs rapidly and can be life-threatening. Current clinical guidelines for anaphylaxis management recommend the use of glucocorticoids as part of the treatment protocol for individuals experiencing this condition. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms associated with the administration of glucocorticoids during anaphylactic episodes. In the previous version of this review, the literature search was conducted up to September 2009. For the updated version, searches were performed in the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) (The Cochrane Library 2011, Issue 3), MEDLINE (Ovid) (1956 to September 2011), EMBASE (Ovid) (1982 to September 2011), and CINAHL (EBSCOhost) (up to September 2011). Additional searches included the UK National Research Register, websites listing ongoing clinical trials, and direct communication with international experts in anaphylaxis to identify unpublished data. The inclusion criteria for this review specified randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared glucocorticoids to any control intervention, such as placebo, adrenaline (epinephrine), antihistamines, or combinations of these treatments. Two independent reviewers assessed the identified articles to determine their eligibility for inclusion in the analysis. No studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified during the review process. As a result, the authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to provide any recommendations regarding the use of glucocorticoids in the treatment of anaphylaxis.
